title: Indian Battery Makers Face Up to 61% Cost Gap With China as Industry Seeks 50% Capex Subsidy
excerpt: An ASSOCHAM–CareEdge study quantifies the disadvantage — and the subsidy ask. The Financial Express names Epsilon Carbon and Himadri as the two stocks positioned for the West's shift beyond China.
body:
• An ASSOCHAM–CareEdge study finds Indian battery component makers face a cost disadvantage of up to 61% against Chinese benchmarks — 61% in cathode material, 53% in anodes, about 40% in cell manufacturing.
  • The industry is seeking a capital subsidy of up to 50%, expanded production-linked incentives and R&D support.
  • The Financial Express picks Epsilon Carbon and Himadri Speciality Chemical as the two Indian stocks positioned if US and European buyers diversify away from China.
  • The catch, per the industry itself: foreign interest has not yet turned into assured purchase volumes for Indian plants.

India's battery component makers say they cannot beat China on cost — yet — and they have put a number on the gap. A study by ASSOCHAM and CareEdge, discussed at an industry session in New Delhi on November 3, finds Indian manufacturers operate at a cost disadvantage of up to 61% against Chinese benchmarks in cathode active material, up to 53% in anode material and roughly 40% in cell manufacturing, according to CNBC-TV18 and pv magazine India.

What the industry is asking for

The industry's response is a request for state support on the same scale as the gap: a capital expenditure subsidy of up to 50% for battery component plants, expansion of production-linked incentives, and funding for research and development. S.M. Vaidya, who chaired the session, made the case plainly: "Where there is substantial value addition, where there is substantial risk taking, where there is lot of capital going in, the government should support them." Those are requests to the government, not announced policy.

The two stocks in the frame

The Financial Express points to two listed Indian companies as the geared-up beneficiaries if Western buyers keep diversifying supply chains beyond China. The first is Epsilon Carbon, whose synthetic graphite anode business the paper credits with roughly ₹4,800 crore in revenue and ₹660 crore in profit after tax in FY26 and about a fifth of the global anode market outside China; its US plant is already exporting to South Korea. The second is Himadri Speciality Chemical, which is investing in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cathode material and silicon-carbon anodes, and has a joint venture with Birla Carbon aimed at battery material for the US, UK and Europe.

The US angle — and the honest caveat

The strategic backdrop is real: US and European battery makers are actively looking for supply chains that do not run through China, and Indian material makers are the obvious alternative at scale. But the industry is candid that interest is not yet orders. Indian executives at the session acknowledged there are no assured purchase volumes from foreign buyers so far — the demand is prospective, and plants built on it need either anchor customers or the subsidy bridge the study proposes. For diaspora investors, that is the correct way to read the story: two well-positioned companies, a genuine policy tailwind, and a 61% cost gap that has to close before the boom is a fact rather than a forecast.
